title: The Running Case: Six Layers of Digital Infrastructure
text: The Running Case: Six Layers of Digital Infrastructure 3 TeleGeography (2026), State of the Network 2026; Ofcom (2025), Connected Nations 2025; ITU (2025); company results releases of 2025 and 2026; SpaceX. Page references are in the notes. Layer What is built How it earns A figure from the evidence Subsea cables Fibre pairs between landing stations on different coasts Sale or exchange of capacity; the main buyers are now content and cloud firms Cables worth over US$14 billion may enter service in 2025 to 2027 Terrestrial fibre Long-haul and city routes, and the last mile to homes and offices Wholesale access for retail providers, under price regulation in the UK Full fibre passes 78% of UK homes; 42% of those have taken it Towers and masts Sites with a structure, land and power for operators' antennas Rent per tenant under long contracts with mobile operators Tenants per tower range from 1.47 to 2.26 across five listed companies Satellites Constellations in low orbit, with ground stations and user terminals Subscriptions to users and capacity to operators Over 110,000 Starlink connections in the UK; design life five years or more Data centres Buildings with power, cooling and connections, let to cloud and other tenants Rent per kilowatt of capacity, on leases of several years Two operators each run over 30 million square feet Interconnection Exchanges and carrier-dense sites where networks meet Port and cross-connection fees The largest exchanges each exceed 14 Tbps at peak

title: Connectivity and Growth: The Evidence on Demand
text: Connectivity and Growth: The Evidence on Demand 4 The base: about 6 billion people, three quarters of the world, were online in 2025; 2.2 billion were not, 96 per cent of them in low- and middle-income countries Growth: a ten point rise in broadband penetration raised annual growth in income per head by 0.9 to 1.5 points in OECD countries from 1996 to 2007 Jobs: the arrival of submarine cables raised the probability of employment in Africa by 3 to 13 per cent in three datasets, a result a 2024 comment says is not robust The cost: connecting the remaining three billion by 2030 was put at US$428 billion in 2020, most of it for infrastructure ITU (2025), Facts and Figures 2025; Czernich et al. (2011), Economic Journal 121(552); Hjort and Poulsen (2018), NBER Working Paper 23582; Roodman (2024), arXiv 2401.13694; ITU (2020), Connecting Humanity, page 12.

title: Fibre to the Home: Coverage Runs Ahead of Take-Up
text: Fibre to the Home: Coverage Runs Ahead of Take-Up 5 Coverage: full fibre reached 78 per cent of UK homes in July 2025, up from 69 per cent a year earlier, and gigabit-capable networks 87 per cent Take-up: 42 per cent of premises that can get full fibre have taken it, 33 per cent of all premises, with rural take-up of 56 per cent above urban at 40 Time: take-up rises with the time since build, from 14 per cent in the first year to 55 per cent after three The builders: Openreach had passed 20 million premises when Ofcom decided in March 2026 and plans 30 million by 2030, while rival networks build alongside it Ofcom (2025), Connected Nations 2025, UK report, Tables 2.5 and 2.6 and pages 4, 6, 11 and 12; Ofcom (2026), Telecoms Access Review 2026-31, Volume 4, page 21.

title: Wholesale Access and the Ladder of Investment
text: Wholesale Access and the Ladder of Investment 6 The idea: regulators let entrants climb from renting the incumbent's service to renting its ducts to building their own network (Cave, 2006) The rule: Openreach must give rivals access to its ducts, and its FTTP 80/20 rental is capped at 18.18 pounds a month for 2026 to 2031 The test: an efficient entrant needs 13.59 to 21.21 pounds a month; the cap sits within that range, towards its upper end The consequence: a second network divides customers: Ofcom assumes 90 per cent take-up for Openreach alone, 60 per cent with an altnet and 30 for the altnet Ofcom (2026), Telecoms Access Review 2026-31, Volume 4, paragraphs 1.116 and 1.117, and Annex 12, paragraph A12.35 and footnote 599; Cave (2006), Telecommunications Policy 30(3-4), 223 to 237.

title: Towers and the Neutral Host
text: Towers and the Neutral Host 7 The model: a tower company rents space and power to several mobile operators, so each added tenant brings rent at little extra cost The range: from 2.26 tenants per tower at Helios Towers to 1.47 at IHS Holding; China Tower reports 1.78 on 2.17 million sites The contracts: Helios has US$5.9 billion of contracted revenue, 98 per cent from large operators, with 6.5 years of initial life remaining on average The risk: IHS lost 3,704 tenants to churn in a year, 2,576 of them in one quarter when a small Nigerian operator changed its contract Helios Towers (30 July 2026); China Tower (11 August 2026); Indus Towers (July 2026, as reported); Cellnex (November 2025, February 2026); IHS Holding (Q2 2026). Periods and definitions differ.

title: Subsea Cables: Content Providers Take the Lead
text: Subsea Cables: Content Providers Take the Lead 8 Scale: international bandwidth demand reached 6.4 petabits a second in 2024, up 29 per cent in the year, slowing from 45 per cent in 2020 Who uses it: content and cloud networks took almost three quarters of demand, and at least 80 per cent on the three busiest routes Who pays: cables worth over US$14 billion may enter service in 2025 to 2027; 2Africa was built by a consortium led by Meta The price: a 100 Gbps wavelength fell 11 per cent a year on average from 2021 to 2024, from 25 per cent on one route to 2 on another TeleGeography (2026), State of the Network 2026, pages 7 to 15; ITU News (2 February 2026); International Cable Protection Committee (2025); Meta Engineering (17 November 2025).

title: Satellites: A Complement with a Short Life
text: Satellites: A Complement with a Short Life 9 The UK: over 110,000 Starlink connections in 2025, from about 87,000; Ofcom has authorised nine non-geostationary licences, seven in low orbit Where: over 12,600 connections are in places without decent fixed or wireless broadband; 27 per cent are where full fibre is available The asset: Starlink satellites are designed for five years or more, so the constellation must be replaced continually The link: a tower company argues that satellites add backhaul demand in rural areas, and cites a forecast that terrestrial networks carry 97 per cent of data in 2040 Ofcom (2025), Connected Nations 2025, UK report, pages 4 and 18; SpaceX, Starlink space safety pages; Helios Towers (2026), H1 results presentation, pages 17 and 28 (company view of an FTI Consulting forecast).

title: Space Assets and the Infrastructure Test
text: Space Assets and the Infrastructure Test 10 Applied to orbit, the working definition from Week 1 separates networks that many users rely on from equipment that serves one owner. Wagner (2026), SSRN 7576078; OECD (2026), The Space Economy at a Glance 2026, pages 14 to 15; HSF Kramer (2026), Space infrastructure; London Economics (2021), GOV.UK; IJGlobal and Flightglobal on Skynet 5; press reports on OneWeb. Classification is mine; see notes. Space asset Network service and asset life Access and funding Navigation and timing (GPS, Galileo) A signal many sectors rely on; the UK benefit was put at £13.6 billion a year Provided by states, free to users Geostationary communications Television, military and weather links; 590 satellites in 2023, designed to last up to 15 years Protected rights through ITU coordination; no price and no cap on positions Low-orbit broadband Over 14,000 operational satellites by end-2025, one operator holding about 60 per cent; Starlink satellites are designed for five years or more National licences; OneWeb bought out of bankruptcy in 2020 by the UK government and Bharti for $1 billion Defence communications (Skynet 5) A government-only network bought as a service PFI contract signed in 2003, about £2.5 billion over 15 years, extended to 2022 Ground stations and spaceports Sites, antennas and launch pads that serve the network The closest fit to conventional investment: EQT's 2024 agreement to buy 80 per cent of Eutelsat's ground stations lapsed in January 2026 A single-customer satellite or a launch vehicle Equipment: no shared network and no enabli

title: Data Centres: The Building, the Power and the Tenant
text: Data Centres: The Building, the Power and the Tenant 11 The business: operators let space, power and connections; Equinix and Digital Realty each run over 30 million square feet, and over 60 providers run more than a million The tenants: Amazon, Google, Meta and Microsoft deployed 16 new data centres in a year and have at least 55 more locations in development The constraint: commercial operators in the top ten markets use about 16 gigawatts; only 22 per cent of sites can supply more than 20 kilowatts a rack, and AI needs 45 to 80 The price: colocation rates of US$400 to US$460 per kilowatt in several hubs, with operators expecting rises of 3 to 5 per cent and power and space the main concern TeleGeography (2026), State of the Network 2026, Data Centers findings, pages 28 to 30. Commercial operators only; the rates are as printed, without a stated period.

title: Three Models of Demand, Technology and Asset Life
text: Three Models of Demand, Technology and Asset Life 14 The three share one structure: a large cost before revenue, revenue that depends on how many use the asset, and a price or a customer base that moves against the owner. Technology enters each differently: through the cost of connecting a customer, through the number of tenants a shared site can hold, and through the price fall that shortens an asset's useful life. Ofcom (2026), Telecoms Access Review 2026-31; Helios Towers (2026); TeleGeography (2026), State of the Network 2026. Interactive pages in web/. Model Layer it describes Question it answers Where the numbers come from 1. Roll-out and break-even price Fixed fibre How many customers must a network connect before it pays, and what does a second network do to the answer? Ofcom's Fibre Cost Model, 2026 2. Tenancy and operating leverage Towers, and any shared passive asset What does each extra tenant add to the return, and what does a tenant leaving take away? Helios Towers, first half 2026 3. Falling prices, growing demand and life Subsea cables, and any capacity asset What is an asset worth when the price of its output falls every year? TeleGeography, State of the Network 2026

title: The Roll-Out Model: Break-Even Price and Take-Up
text: The Roll-Out Model: Break-Even Price and Take-Up 15 The structure: a build cost per home passed up front, a connection cost as customers join, a running cost, and a price per connected line per month The calibration: on Ofcom's low- and high-cost inputs the break-even price is 12.69 and 21.55 pounds, against Ofcom's published 13.30 and 20.76 The sensitivity: take-up is the swing factor: for the low-cost entrant 11.21 pounds at 55 per cent, 12.69 at 40 and 14.51 at 30 The comparison: the price cap of 18.18 pounds lies inside the range, towards its upper end Ofcom (2026), Telecoms Access Review 2026-31, Annex 11, Tables A11.5 and A11.6 and paragraph A11.161, page 233; Volume 4, page 20; Ofcom (2025), Connected Nations 2025, page 12. The model is mine.

title: Break-Even Price, Take-Up and Overbuild
text: Break-Even Price, Take-Up and Overbuild 16 Alone: on Ofcom's central Area 3 costs, a network that has the area to itself needs 13.35 pounds a month, and earns 9.2 per cent a year at the cap price of 18.18 With a second network: keeping two thirds of the customers, it needs 16.11 pounds and earns 6.9 per cent The rival: a network with a third needs 24.39 pounds and earns 3.3 per cent at the cap price, below its cost of capital The lesson: a second network divides customers rather than adding them, so the cost of duplication falls on the investors of one or both, or on customers Ofcom (2026), Telecoms Access Review 2026-31, Annex 12, Tables and paragraphs A12.21, A12.34, A12.35, Table A12.5 and footnote 599 (pages 239 to 243). The model and the real rate are mine. Interactive page in web/.

title: Tenancy and Operating Leverage
text: Tenancy and Operating Leverage 17 The anchor: 2.26 tenants per tower, an EBITDA margin of 55 per cent and a return on invested capital of 14.4 per cent, from Helios Towers' first half of 2026 The leverage: if half of site cost is fixed, each added tenant brings about US$21 thousand of EBITDA to a site with US$166 thousand of capital, about 13 points of return The evidence: growth capital of US$316 million in 2023 to 2025 added US$112 million of free cash flow, over 30 per cent, against 14.4 per cent on all capital The risk: the same arithmetic runs in reverse when a tenant leaves, as IHS found when it lost 3,704 tenants to churn in a year Helios Towers plc (2026), results for the six months to 30 June 2026, pages 1, 2 and 15; H1 2026 results presentation, pages 7 and 13; IHS Holding (2026). The split of site cost is my assumption.

title: Price Decline, Demand Growth and Asset Life
text: Price Decline, Demand Growth and Asset Life 19 The structure: revenue is price times the smaller of demand and capacity; price falls every year, demand grows, and an upgrade raises capacity at a fraction of the build cost The data: TeleGeography: route demand up 29 per cent in 2024; the price of a 100 Gbps wavelength down 11 per cent a year, from 2 to 25 by route The result: with no upgrade revenue peaks in year 9 and falls, and the value is minus 31 million; two upgrades move it to 111 million The route: at a 2 per cent fall the value with upgrades is 1856 million, at 25 per cent minus 488 TeleGeography (2026), State of the Network 2026, pages 7, 13 and 14. The cost, revenue and upgrade parameters and the model are mine and are not estimates for any cable.
